title: Coding Interview Field Guide
description: A coding-round field guide built around invariants, data-structure choice, readable Python/JavaScript/Java implementation, and proof under time pressure.

sections.title: Mental Model: Invariant First
sections.summary: A coding interview is not a template recall test. It is a state-management test: identify the state, protect the invariant, and code so the state is obvious.
items: Restate the input, output, and one concrete example before solving.
Ask only questions that change code: size, sortedness, duplicates, negatives, mutation, tie behavior, and empty input.
Say the brute force baseline to expose the bottleneck.
Name the repeated work: lookup, range computation, ordering, graph revisit, or overlapping subproblem.
Choose the data structure and say exactly what it stores.
State the invariant in one sentence before implementation.
Code with explainable variable names that match the invariant.
Test the invariant with sample, empty/singleton, duplicate, impossible, and boundary cases.
Close with final complexity and the trade-off the chosen structure introduced.

sections.title: Cheatsheet: Data Structure Triggers
sections.summary: Map prompt pressure to the structure that removes the expensive operation.
items: Repeated lookup, complements, counts, anagrams, first unique -> map or set.
Sorted input with pair/triplet/partition pressure -> two pointers.
Longest or shortest contiguous range with a condition -> sliding window.
Range totals, subarray equals k, immutable queries -> prefix sum plus map.
Next greater/smaller, histogram, temperatures -> monotonic stack.
Top k, merge k lists, running median, scheduling priority -> heap.
Linked-list cycle, middle, or intersection -> fast/slow pointers.
Shortest unweighted path, nearest cell, level spread -> BFS.
Components, all paths, tree aggregation -> DFS with visited or parent guard.
Dependencies and build order -> topological sort.
Dynamic connectivity -> union-find.
Count/min/max over repeated choices -> dynamic programming.
All combinations/permutations/subsets -> backtracking with choose/explore/unchoose.

sections.title: Cheatsheet: Complexity and Proof
sections.summary: Use constraints to reject bad plans and use the invariant to prove the good one.
items: n <= 20: exponential search may be acceptable if pruning is clear.
n <= 1,000: O(n^2) is often the ceiling.
n <= 100,000: target O(n log n) or O(n).
n >= 1,000,000: target O(n), O(log n), or streaming state.
Graphs: traversal should usually be O(V + E).
DP runtime is number of states times transition cost.
Sorting costs O(n log n); only pay it if ordering unlocks a simpler invariant.
Proof language: each item enters/leaves once, each edge is visited once, heap size stays k, or each memo state solves once.

title: Coding Interview Strategy
description: Concrete phrases and control points for the live round.

sections.title: Opening Script
items: 'Let me restate: given [input], return [output], optimizing for [goal].'
'Can input be empty? Are values unique? Are negatives possible? Is the array sorted? Can I mutate it?'
'For n around [size], O(...) is likely too slow, so I will target O(...).'
'I'll start with a brute force baseline, then optimize the repeated work.'

sections.title: Invariant Lines
sections.summary: Use these to explain correctness while coding.
items: Sliding window: 'At every step, the window is the largest valid window ending at right.'
Two pointers: 'Because the array is sorted, moving left increases the sum and moving right decreases it.'
Heap: 'The heap keeps only the best k candidates seen so far.'
BFS: 'The first time we pop a node, we have the shortest distance in an unweighted graph.'
DP: 'dp[i] stores the best answer for prefix i, so later states reuse solved prefixes.'
Backtracking: 'The path is the current partial choice; after recursion I undo the choice.'

sections.title: If You Get Stuck
sections.summary: Use a reset protocol instead of going silent.
items: Generate a 3-item example and trace the desired output.
Name the bottleneck in brute force: lookup, repeated compute, ordering, or choice explosion.
Ask: 'Is there a monotonic property here?' If yes, consider binary search/two pointers/monotonic stack.
Ask: 'What state would I need if I processed left to right?' If small, consider hash/prefix/DP.
Say: 'I have a partial approach; let me validate it on the example before coding.'

title: Pattern Playbook
description: Trigger words, templates, and gotchas for common coding interview patterns.

sections.title: Arrays and Strings
sections.summary: Most array/string problems are state tracking problems.
items: Hash map template: for each x, check needed value before inserting x when matching pairs by index.
Sliding window template: expand right, update state, while invalid shrink left, record answer after valid.
Prefix sum template: running += nums[i]; answer += count[running - target]; count[running]++.
Two pointers template: initialize l=0,r=n-1; move the pointer that can improve the sorted condition.
Monotonic stack template: while stack top is worse than current, pop and resolve top using current as next boundary.
Gotcha: with negative numbers, fixed-size or sum-based sliding window often fails; use prefix sums instead.

sections.title: Graphs and Trees
items: DFS recursion: subtree aggregation, path enumeration, connected components.
BFS queue: shortest number of edges, level order, nearest target, grid spread time.
Topological sort: indegree map + queue of zero indegree nodes; cycle if processed count < n.
Union-find: path compression + union by rank; use when edges arrive and connectivity is queried repeatedly.
Tree DP: return two values when node has include/exclude choices, e.g. rob/not rob.
Gotcha: mark visited when enqueueing, not when dequeueing, to avoid duplicate queue entries.

sections.title: DP and Backtracking
sections.summary: The hard part is naming state and transition.
items: 1D DP: dp[i] usually means best/count/possible for prefix ending at i.
2D DP: dp[i][j] usually means best answer using first i and first j, or interval i..j.
Knapsack trigger: choose/not choose items with capacity or target sum.
LIS trigger: sequence order plus increasing condition; O(n^2) DP or O(n log n) tails.
Backtracking duplicate rule: sort first, then skip nums[i] if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1].
Memo key should include every variable that changes future choices. Missing one causes false sharing.

checklists.title: Pattern Gotchas
items: negative numbers break sum window
duplicates need sorted skip
BFS mark on enqueue
DP base row/column
heap size capped at k
binary search loop invariant

title: Optimization and Testing
description: Concrete ways to turn a correct idea into an efficient, defensible solution.

sections.title: Optimization Map
sections.summary: Replace the expensive operation, not the whole solution.
items: Nested membership check -> hash set/map.
Repeated range sum -> prefix sum.
Repeated subtree/path result -> memoization.
Need top k only -> min heap of size k, not full sort.
Need ordered dynamic min/max -> heap or balanced tree, not repeated scan.
Search answer with monotonic feasibility -> binary search on answer.
Many string prefixes -> trie.
Many interval overlaps -> sort endpoints or sweep line.

sections.title: Test Case Menu
items: Array: empty, one item, two items, duplicates, all same, negatives, sorted, reverse sorted.
String: empty, one char, repeated chars, unicode if relevant, overlapping matches.
Graph: disconnected, cycle, self-loop, no path, multiple shortest paths.
Tree: null, single node, skewed, balanced, duplicate values.
Intervals: touching endpoints, nested intervals, same start, no overlap, complete overlap.
DP: zero capacity/target, impossible target, exactly one solution, repeated choices.

sections.title: Complexity Language
items: 'Time is O(n) because each index enters and leaves the window once.'
'Time is O(V + E) because every node and edge is processed once.'
'Time is O(n log k) because each item can cause one heap operation on a heap of size k.'
'Space is O(n) for the map plus O(h) recursion stack, where h is tree height.'
'The sort dominates at O(n log n); the scan after sorting is O(n).'
'Memoization has O(states * transition cost), not just O(n).'

title: Coding Practice Plan
description: A concrete practice loop for pattern recognition and interview execution.

sections.title: Two-Week Drill
sections.summary: Repeatable schedule for one focused sprint.
items: Day 1: arrays/hash maps, 5 untimed, write triggers after each.
Day 2: two pointers/sliding window, 5 untimed, trace every pointer move.
Day 3: stack/heap/binary search, 5 mixed.
Day 4: trees/graphs BFS/DFS, 5 mixed.
Day 5: DP/backtracking, 4 slower problems, write state definition first.
Day 6: 3 timed mixed problems at 35 minutes each.
Day 7: redo every miss from memory.
Week 2: same rotation, but every problem is timed and spoken aloud.

sections.title: Review Log Fields
sections.summary: Do not just mark solved. Capture the failure mode.
items: Missed pattern: what trigger should have revealed it?
Bug type: off-by-one, stale state, bad base case, duplicate handling, wrong comparator.
Complexity gap: what operation made it too slow?
Hint needed: what was the smallest hint that unlocked it?
Redo date: schedule 2 days later and 7 days later.

sections.title: Ready for Real Rounds
items: Solve medium array/string in 25 minutes with explanation.
Solve medium graph/tree in 35 minutes with tests.
Can name invariant before coding for 8 common patterns.
Can recover from a wrong approach without freezing.
Can produce 4 edge cases without interviewer prompting.

checklists.title: Daily Reps
items: 1 warmup easy
